utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are here today to have a Pre-Trial Conference under Rule 73 bis. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Re for the Prosecution with Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and case manager, Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. For the Haradinaj Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ben Emmerson, lead counsel for Mr. Haradinaj, together with Rodney Dixon and Susan Park.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Haradinaj, can you hear me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Appearances for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, lead counsel, and with me Colleen Rohan and Mr. Bart Willemsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Balaj, can you hear me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can hear you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Richard Harvey and Ms. Antoniette Trapani, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brahimaj, can you hear me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. This case was referred to this Trial Chamber on the 15th of January, 2007, just after the amendment to the indictment was completed. An informal meeting, an informal introductory meeting was held between the parties and the Judges in my chambers on the 26th of January 2007. The main issues discussed during this meeting was the reduction of the indictment. Ultimately, the Chamber decided not to order the Prosecution to reduce the indictment. This was a decision filed on the 22nd of February of this year. During that same meeting, the Chamber granted the Prosecution an additional 3.000 words for its pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You Honour, I do apologise for interrupting. It is very difficult to hear. I don't have the benefit of earphones over here. I don't know if anything could be done about the volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm surprised you don't have the benefit of earphones because there are so many lying around. I would offer my loud voice, but it's not nice for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's much nicer to hear you viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I start speaking very loudly, which I can do without any problem, then it is not pleasant for the interpreters either, because it will be loud in their ears as well. So I think we should adapt to either hearing by microphone or not; but if there is any problem, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the first item on the agenda -- you've received an agenda, I take it, with all the main points on it. So we have dealt with the introduction. If there's any question or any issue to be raised, please do so. If not, we'll move on to the second paragraph, that is, the pleas on the revised second indictment. It is the revised second indictment of the 10th of November, 2006, which was confirmed, as I just said, on the 12th of January, 2007. Pursuant to Rule 50(B), a further appearance must be held for each of the accused to enter pleas against counts 1 and 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29, 31, 35, and 37 of the current indictment. Now, I had in mind just to mention these numbers but -- and then -- because I understood that the Defence would be agreeable to just mentioning the numbers and then the accused to enter pleas on these counts. But for a specific reason, I thought it would be better to go a bit more in detail. Before I invited accused to enter a plea on these counts, I'd like to have a clarification from the Prosecution, mainly on count 35. Count 35, where a crime against humanity or persecution or, alternatively, a crime against humanity, imprisonment, torture, rape, and other inhumane acts, are charged. We see that all accused, and I'm looking at the lines under paragraph 114. Do you see that, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've found it? It reads there that by these actions or omissions, Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, Lahi Brahimaj, committed, as part of a JCE, and then counts 35 in two alternatives follows 36 then 37; and then it says in the alternative, Idriz Balaj committed or planned the commission of the crimes described in count 36 and 37. Now, 35 is not included. We're talking about the very last line of the indictment itself. If, however, I look at paragraph 23 of the indictment, where it is explained to what extent the accused are held responsible, and 23 specifically for Mr. Balaj, it says that "Mr. Balaj is, apart from responsibility as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, is individually criminally responsible for his acts and omissions in that he planned, instigated, committed, or aided and abetted the crimes described and charged in" and then a number of counts follow, including 35. But I don't find that set out in relation to 35 under paragraph 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I missed a word when someone coughed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here we see in 23 it says that Mr. Balaj is individually responsible for planning, instigating, et cetera, and then it gives the whole list, including 35; however, on -- under paragraph 114, the very last line of the indictment - surprises are always kept to the very end - it mentions only 36, 37, and not 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. All I can say is it appears Your Honours' careful rereading of the indictment has spotted a proofreading error which seems to have escaped the previous Trial Chamber, the combined Prosecution team, everyone else, and it should, of course, in my submission say 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I don't know how -- well, the Defence has not complained about it either, about its inconsistency. I would be a bit worried about it; but, of course, it's only Mr. Balaj's defence which is affected by it. How is this understood between the parties? That the committing or planning, which is not the full list of paragraph 23 where it speaks of planning, instigating, committing, or aiding and abetting. Has the Balaj Defence read the commission, or planning the commission, of the crimes to include 35 or to exclude 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've moved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've moved to the right. In all honesty, although having noted the distinction between paragraphs 23 and 114, I think it would be fair to say that in the manner in which the indictment is pled, it would include 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I take it that you do not oppose this view?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no. And we, of course, would make an oral submission to amend the indictment to include the number 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to amend or to correct an inconsistency in the indictment where it has been clearly announced in paragraph 23 that 35 would be included in the non-JCE responsibility as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. I believe that had I raised this in the future when I intended to raise it, the Chamber's response would most probably be that it would be a non-fatal variance and that the notice provisions were sufficient under paragraph 23 for purposes of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we, just for practical reasons, could we understand your last remark as an oral application for permission to correct the indictment to the extent that count 35 would be included in the very last line of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Balaj Defence, and I don't think that any of the parties would have an interest in responding to it, since the Balaj Defence does not oppose, permission is granted, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can move on to inviting the accused to enter pleas, not on all counts, because some of them have not added any charges. I'm, therefore, following the decision of the Trial Chamber, which it says on which counts pleas have to be entered. I suggest to do it the following way: I'll read, in an abbreviated version, each of the counts. I will always announce who is responsible or is allegedly responsible under JCE or also under individually, and I'll mention exactly what is charged for each of the individual accused. From the agreement to read all the numbers and then have pleas, I would not be surprised if it would be all not guilty pleas. Therefore, I will read -- if on any of these charges one of the accused would consider to enter a guilty plea, I would like to be interrupted; if not, I will just continue and invite the accused, at the very end, to enter a plea on all of the counts, in the modes of responsibility as specifically mentioned, to enter a plea. Is that agreeable to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then count 1 is a crime against humanity, persecution, or, in the alternative, a crime against humanity, torture, and other inhumane acts. Count 2, a violation of the laws or customs of war, cruel treatment and torture and outrages upon personal dignity. On counts 1 and 2, all of the accused are charged with responsibility under 7(1), a joint criminal enterprise. Ramush Haradinaj, also in the alternative, that he ordered, instigated, or aided and abetted the commissions of the crime under counts 1 and 2. Count 3, a crime against humanity, persecution, or, in the alternative, a crime against humanity, torture, and other inhumane acts. Count 4, a violation of the laws or customs of war -- and there I missed the -- let me just ... So count 4, a violation of the laws or customs of war, cruel treatment and torture. All accused are charged with responsibility as participants of a joint criminal enterprise. Ramush Haradinaj also charged with, in the alternative, that he committed or aided and abetted the commission of the crimes described in counts 3 and 4. Count 5, a crime against humanity, persecution, or, alternatively, a crime against humanity, imprisonment, torture, or other inhumane acts. Count 6, a violation of the laws or customs of war, cruel treatment and torture. For counts 5 and 6, all accused exclusively charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. Count 16, a violation of the laws or customs of war, murder, and cruel treatment. All accused on count 16, charged with responsibility as participants in the joint criminal enterprise. Ramush Haradinaj, in the alternative, also charged with having committed or planned or aided and abetted the commission of this crime. Count 18, a violation of the laws or customs of war, murder and cruel treatment. Count 19, a crime against humanity, persecution, or, in the alternative, a crime against humanity, murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts. Count 20, a violation of the laws or customs of war, murder and cruel treatment and torture. On these three counts, 18, 19, and 20, all accused charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. In the alternative, Idriz Balaj also charged with having committed or aided and abetted the commission of these crimes. Count 21, a crime against humanity, persecution, or, in the alternative, a crime against humanity, murder. Count 22, a violation of the laws or customs of war, murder. All three accused charged exclusively with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. Count 23, a crime against humanity, persecution, or, alternatively, a crime against humanity, murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts. Count 24, a violation of the laws or customs of war, murder and cruel treatment and torture. All accused charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. Alternatively, Ramush Haradinaj, that he committed or aided and abetted the commission of these crimes. Idriz Balaj, in the alternative, that he committed or aided and abetted the commission of these crimes. And Lahi Brahimaj, that he ordered, instigated, or aided and abetted the commission of these crimes described in counts 23 and 24. Count 26, a violation of the laws or customs of war, murder and cruel treatment. All accused charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. In the alternative, Lahi Brahimaj, also that he ordered, instigated, or aided and abetted the commission of the crimes described in count 26. Count 27, a crime against humanity, persecution, or, alternatively, a crime against humanity, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts. Count 28, a violation of the laws or customs of war, cruel treatment, and torture. All accused charged with responsibility as participants in the joint criminal enterprise, but in the alternative, Lahi Brahimaj, also that he committed or aided and abetted the commission of the crimes described in counts 27 and 28. Count 29, a crime against humanity, persecution; in the alternative, a crime against humanity, murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts. All accused charged exclusively with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. Count 31, a crime against humanity, persecution; in the alternative, a crime against humanity, murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts. All accused charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise, and in the alternative, Ramush Haradinaj, that he aided and abetted the commission of the crime; Idriz Balaj, that he committed or planned, instigated, or aided and abetted the commission of the crime; Lahi Brahimaj, that he committed or that he planned, instigated, or aided and abetted the commission of the crime described in count 31. I'll now come to count 35, which I'll put in accordance with the correction for which leave has been granted already; that is, count 35, a crime against humanity, persecution; in the alternative, a crime against humanity, imprisonment, torture, rape, and other inhumane acts. All accused charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise. In the alternative, Idriz Balaj, also charged with having committed or having planned the crime described in count 35. Count 37, a violation of the laws or customs of war, cruel treatment, and torture. All accused charged with responsibility as participants in a joint criminal enterprise under Article 7(1) of the indictment -- of the Statute. In the alternative, Idriz Balaj, also that he committed or that he planned the commission of this crime described in count 37. Having read the counts on which you will now be invited to enter a plea, I'd first like to invite Mr. Ramush Haradinaj to enter a plea on all the counts I just mentioned for responsibility as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise, and, where specified, as responsible in another mode under Article 7(1), in the alternative, that is included. Mr. Haradinaj, how do you plead to these counts? THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ: Honourable Judge, I plead not guilty and I am offended by this indictment. [Interpretation] I declare myself not guilty, and I am very offended by these accusations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haradinaj, I invited you to enter a plea, not to give any additional comment. Will you please carefully listen to what I ask you, and then ask leave to make any further comments, if you think that you need to do so. Madam Registrar, could you please put on the record the plea of not guilty entered by Mr. Haradinaj on the counts I just read to him. You may be seated, Mr. Haradinaj. Then Mr. Balaj. Mr. Balaj, you are also invited to enter a plea on the counts I've just read. Again, on all of the counts, responsibility as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, and on those counts, where specified, also responsibility under another mode of commission, under Article 7(1). How do you plead to all these counts? THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am completely innocent of all charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please record the plea of not guilty entered by Mr. Balaj. Then Mr. Brahimaj. Mr. Brahimaj, may I invite you also to enter a plea on all the counts I just read to you, all of them in which you are charged with responsibility as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise and on those specifically mentioned, also charged -- where you are charged with another mode of committing these crimes, under Article 7(1), as specified. How do you plea to all these counts? THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] I am completely innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please record the plea of not guilty entered by Mr. Brahimaj on all the counts. This was item 2 on the agenda. I'd like now to move on to item 3 on the agenda, which is pending motions. On the 22nd of February of this year, the Chamber has notified the parties by e-mail that it had denied the Prosecution's urgent motion requesting the revocation of UNMIK's decision-making power on matters pertaining to Mr. Haradinaj's provisional release. The written reasons for this decision will be filed with the Registry shortly. Moving on to 3(b). The Chamber recalls that Mr. Haradinaj's motion for a subpoena for certain notes, a motion filed on 12 October 2006, has been put on hold. The Chamber will not act on this motion unless requested to do so by the parties. Moving on to 3(c). The Chamber has received Mr. Balaj's Rule 72 motion, as well as the Prosecution's response to that motion. We will decide the matter in due course. Under 3(d), we find a confidential Prosecution application for subpoena for a document, which was dated the 26th of February of this year. Although the motion was filed confidentially, there's no need to go into private session; I take it, Mr. Re, that you would agree with that. The Defence for Mr. Haradinaj filed a response, I think it was, yesterday which essentially renders the subpoena request moot. This is also what the Prosecution, meanwhile, submitted, that in the expectation that the document will be received by the Prosecution, I think it was, early next week, that you would withdraw the motion. The Registry is instructed in this respect to change the status of the three filings, until now, from confidential to public. I now move on to item 3(e). The Chamber has received the Prosecution's Rule 92 bis motion dated the 19th of February, 2007. Yesterday, the Chamber also received a response by the Haradinaj Defence but not, I think, from the Defence of the other accused. Is that correct, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I believe you will be receiving a response on behalf of Mr. Balaj momentarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by that I mean within the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For some people, a moment is a second; for others, it's ten years. Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll be receiving a response a few moments after Mr. Guy-Smith's in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that some 20 or 30 years after that, or a couple of hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It is more likely to be tomorrow rather than today, Your Honour, but it will be by the end of the day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. The Chamber, of course, will first receive these responses and then decide the matter in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll move on to 3(f). The Chamber is in receipt of an exchange of views between Mr. Balaj's Defence and the Prosecution on the subject of expert reports and on notice given pursuant to Rule 94 bis. In the last filing in this series, the Defence for Mr. Balaj asked the Chamber permission to file a consolidated response once the Prosecution has completed its disclosure of expert reports. Mr. Guy-Smith, the request is hereby granted. Is there any other matter the parties would like to raise under this heading of experts? And the Chamber is aware, although we have not read anything yet, that counsel for Haradinaj has filed a submission on 94 bis, I think it was, today or yesterday. We haven't read it yet, but we are aware that it was filed. So in addition to what has been filed, is there any need to further address this matter of expert reports? I see, Mr. Emmerson, you are nodding no; Mr. Guy-Smith; Mr. Haradinaj. Then we will move on to 3(g). On the 4th of January in the year 2002, protective measures were granted to witnesses K5 and K6 in the case of the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic. In particular, the Milosevic Chamber ordered that their identities not be disclosed to any members of the public, including "the accused and Defence counsel in other cases or proceedings before this Tribunal." On the 27th of September, 2006, Trial Chamber II ordered that the protective measures previously granted to the two witnesses continue to have effect in the current case. On the 20th of February, 2007, the Prosecution submitted a motion requesting the Trial Chamber to vary the protective measures granted to witnesses K5 and K6 so as to give Defence counsel access to the unredacted testimony of the two witnesses. Rule 75(I) allows this Chamber to deal with an application to "rescind, vary, or augment protective measures." The Defence has not objected to the Prosecution's condition that full disclosure be made to Defence counsel alone, and not to the accused or to any other members of the Defence teams. I'd first like to verify whether this is still the position taken by the Defence. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, the position of the Defence is that the material should, in principle, be available to the accused as well, particularly since the purpose of disclosing it to counsel is to enable the Defence, in due course, to make application to adduce the evidence, if appropriate. However, if the Trial Chamber is inclined to agree with the position taken by the Prosecution, then we are content to proceed on the basis that the material be disclosed to counsel only as an interim measure, subject to any further application that may be made to the Trial Chamber, if, having seen the unredacted material, counsel consider that an application ought to be made to introduce the material into evidence. May I just make two short points of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you before I -- you say an application should be made only if the material had to be introduced in evidence; also, to -- if you considered the material relevant, to discuss with the client whether or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or is it only if you decided on your own that it needed to be introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the important point is it would require a further application to the Trial Chamber on one or other ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two short points of clarification. It is not identification that is in issue so far as the Defence is concerned. What is sought is the redactions of those parts of the material which remain redacted and which, in the case of the testimony, was given in closed session. So what is not sought is revelation of the details of the identities of the individuals or their whereabouts. I simply make that point for the sake of clarification. Secondly, and again it's purely a matter of formality and I don't need to go into it in any detail, I think I'm right in saying that the order Your Honour referred to, having been made in September of last year, granted the access to the de-redacted material, and the Prosecution subsequently applied for a variation of that order so as to keep the material which is currently redacted confidential. And it was in the context of that motion that the Prosecution made the suggestion that it has made. And the third matter is simply a matter of clarification. Up until this point in time, where orders have been made - and there have been one or two - for the disclosure of material to counsel for the accused, it has been agreed between the parties and sanctioned by the Trial Chamber that that expression should extend to legal assistants instructed by the accused. And may we ask that the same principle should apply in respect to this material since inevitably it will be handled by legal assistants, unless very special arrangements are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it only those legal assistants which duly appear on the list of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, and their identities are already established with the Prosecution in respect to de-redacted forensic to the materials to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also under the obligation?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Also under the same obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Mr. Guy-Smith, anything to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would only add two things. One is I think it will become important that, coupled with the de-redacted testimony, we also receive the statements of K5 and K6 in a de-redacted form, because it is very clear from a review of the redacted testimony that we have at this time that there is a great deal of conversation and examination concerning those statements as well. And I think it's necessary, for a complete picture, to have both documents. The only other matter would be a deadline for receipt of the information would be requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey, would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I adopt everything that's been said by both previous counsel and I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have the pleasure of being third which now and then saves a couple of words. Mr. Re, two issues. The first, Mr. Guy-Smith asks you to disclose statements as well and; second, he suggests that the Chamber imposes a deadline. Could you express yourself on the two issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I seek some clarification from Mr. Guy-Smith? When you say "statements," are you referring to Rule 92 bis exhibits in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am referring to the statements alluded and discussed during the examination of both K5 and K6. Further than that, I cannot go at this time, since I'm unclear as to the precise manner in which those statements were introduced into the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I suggest that, with the material in hand, that Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Re, during the next break, will try to identify what statements we're exactly talking about; then inform the Chamber about it. And I think talking about deadlines, if we do not know yet what statements we're talking about, it might not be a good idea. So to revisit the matter after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly. Just in relation to the matter, could I set out the Prosecution's position in case there's any misunderstanding. The redactions to which my colleagues were referring, of course, relate to the identity of the witnesses. Those are the only matters that I'm aware of that have been redacted from the material, which was on the Milosevic transcript in relation to witnesses K5 and K6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there seems to be a difference of opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would beg to differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The identity of the witness, I think, would take from the standpoint of a redaction but a few lines. We still have massive redactions contained in the transcripts of testimony that we have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you never know whether the whole family is described.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's very possible, Your Honour. I really have no way of determining that. I'm happy, once again, to sit down with Mr. Re and discuss this matter. Perhaps we can thrash it through and come to a point where we have an understanding, precisely that which has been hidden, whether it is more than identification or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber will hear about it as well, and I apologise for having spoiled your break already in advance. Therefore, then, we'll revisit 3(h) after the break. The next item is the Prosecution request, found under 3(h), for guidance on question of disclosure of statements of witnesses whom the Prosecution no longer intends to call. The request was filed on the 15th of February. The Chamber has decided this matter and will now deliver its decision orally, so this is the decision on the Prosecution's request for guidance of the 15th of February, 2007. In a motion filed on the 15th of February, 2007, the Prosecution requested guidance from the Chamber on whether it must disclose the unredacted statements of protected persons whom it no longer intends to call to trial. The Prosecution's request came two weeks after the expiry of the deadline for full disclosure. On the 19th and the 21st of February, counsel for Mr. Balaj and for Mr. Haradinaj filed their positions on the matter. To date, according to the information made available to the Chamber, statements of seven of these persons have not been fully disclosed. The statements were used as supporting materials for the indictment. Rule 66(A)(i) requires disclosure of the supporting material which accompanied the indictment. Both the Prosecution's initial request for protective measures of the 7th of April, 2005, and the previous Chamber's decision of the 20th of May, 2005, that granted these initial protective measures dealt specifically with the disclosure obligations under Rule 66(A)(i). The protective measures were granted under Rules 69 and 75, which do not make full disclosure contingent on testimony at trial. Moreover, the previous Chamber's decisions and orders requiring the Prosecution to disclose the unredacted statements no later than 30 days before trial were not made conditional on the protected persons being called to trial. The Prosecution has not provided any reasons for the redactions to remain in place. In particular, it has not argued that this would be necessary for the safety of the protected persons. The Chamber also notes that the Defence has already been informed of the identities of these persons. The Prosecution is, therefore, directed to immediately and fully disclose all remaining statements that were used as supporting materials for the indictment. This concludes the Chamber's decision, or, I should say, the guidance of the Chamber, including an order to immediately and fully disclose. We will then move on to 3(i). That is Mr. Balaj's motion to order UNMIK to lift Rule 70 confidentiality from certain documents. The Chamber invites the Prosecution to update the Chamber on the progress UNMIK is making on reassessing the material that is the subject of Mr. Balaj's motion. Mr. Re, where does UNMIK stand, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: UNMIK's position is that any witness who has agreed to testify to -- agreed to testify for the Prosecution and in respect of whom they have statements, they will authorise us to disclose those statements to the Defence. In relation to Rule 68, UNMIK assures the Prosecution that it is aware of the Prosecution's obligations under Rule 68. And we are at this very moment attempting to persuade UNMIK that certain material should be disclosed to the Defence, and UNMIK is contacting, I think, three people in Kosovo to speak to them about the security implications of disclosing certain information to the Defence. That's going on this week. I'm saying we've identified three potential pieces of Rule 68 information, material that we have that UNMIK has given us, and we have -- we are endeavouring to have them provide us with the Rule 70 -- provide the clearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say you expect a response early next week? No, you say that's going on this week, which of course would make us expect that at least matters would be clarified by the beginning of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I hope so. There is communication between the OTP and UNMIK. I hope so. We're on the telephone to them; we're exchanging correspondence. Our investigators are also speaking to those people. We're doing all that we can humanly do, given the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this update. Is there any need to respond to the situation, as just explained by Mr. Re, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Mr. Guy-Smith's application. I will let him respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. Mr. Guy-Smith, it might take me a couple of days, but then I'll try not to make similar mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not mind periodically for Ben to respond to my applications. That's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Re's present update raises a number of considerations, and I will ask, first of all, whether or not any of the witnesses who the Prosecution expects to call within the next two weeks are witnesses for whom there are statements from UNMIK. That seems to me to be the most immediate of concerns that I would have. I don't know whether or not you can respond to that. Before I go any further, I think that's probably the first order of business, since we have a trial to attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, Mr. Guy-Smith would, first of all, like to know whether any of these witnesses would be -- would appear soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honour can give me one moment, I need to clarify something with my colleague here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Happily, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that's heartening. My second question, then, would be, really, whether Mr. Re is in a position at this point to identify for us those witnesses who have agreed to testify for the Prosecution who have spoken with UNMIK or UNMIK representatives; and, along with that, when we can look forward to seeing the material with regard to those witnesses. And the reason I'm asking this question at this time is because the files, as I understand them to be - and much of the information is anecdotal and some of the information is specific with regard to my experience in a prior case in which we dealt with UNMIK files - is that these files are relatively voluminous; often deal with repeated contacts with the same witness; often deal with contacts in which there is, in fact, a joint effort for investigative purposes by the Office of the Prosecutor and UNMIK so that the actual investigative efforts may, indeed, be somewhat less than a strict Rule 70 situation. And further, it is my understanding - and I may well be wrong but I think I'm not - that with regard to each of the specific counts for which my client is charged, there is a file, which is an active file, in which investigations have been done by UNMIK; and that information, independent of or in addition to any witness who has agreed to testify, would be relevant to properly and adequately defend Mr. Balaj. So I think we're going to be ultimately in a position where - although I'm heartened by the information that UNMIK at this point apparently is willing to hand over - we're going to be requesting further information. I want to alert you to that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Re to respond, Mr. Guy-Smith, is Mr. Re aware of what file you are now alluding to? Did you communicate that with him? Did you say, "I understand, I may be wrong," but you think you're not, that this and this investigation has resulted in a file to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hope springs eternal and I believe that he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would have told him, he would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now just guessing on whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, the reason I put it in those terms, Your Honour, is as follows: We've been having a fair amount of give and take on this issue, and part of the difficulty that we have had has been, very simply, this: I have asked, for example, all files with regard to counts 1 and 2. Mr. Re has said, and others before him have said, Well, we're not in a position to tell you whether any files exist with regard to counts 1 and 2 because if we did such a thing that would be, in our estimation, a potential violation of the rule. So we've spoken about it in the most generic of terms, but I'm sure that through the number of conversations that Mr. Re and I have had, as well as conversations that I've had with prior prosecutors that have been involved in this matter - and there have been a number of them - that my position is quite clear and they are very clear what we seek and know what files we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that there are two issues. The first one, you'd like to know which witnesses would have already agreed to testify, which I take it, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that as soon as the Prosecution enters into an agreement with a witness, a witness protected until then under Rule 70(B), I would say, that we are not in a position anymore that the information shall not be given -- is not to be given in evidence. So I take it that such an agreement would be made only if the entity providing the information would have agreed to that, because otherwise we are leaving the area use solely for the purpose of generating new evidence, rather than the information to be introduced into evidence. But this is my preliminary interpretation of Rule 70(B). Second issue is that Mr. Guy-Smith alludes to a file that, in his opinion, exists, and he more or less announces that he might further pursue that matter. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information to which my learned colleague, Mr. Guy-Smith, refers which we are endeavouring to disclose to the Defence is not relevant for quite some time in the case, not until towards the end of the case. I know what he's talking about; he knows what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the only ones who do not know what you're talking about are we, but that's a party-driven system, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am sorry. We are constrained. There are Rule 70 constraints we have here. I can -- I can talk to my colleagues in the break, as much as I can. I'm not sure that there's anything I can put before the Trial Chamber at this precise moment, other than to say that we are working with UNMIK to try and provide -- to obtain provider clearance in relation to certain material we've identified, but it relates to matters well into the trial, a long way down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Guy-Smith is also, at least if I've understood him well, is saying that "if there is an agreement with some witnesses, to call them, could we then at least receive that information without further delay?" And I suggested such an agreement partly could be made if there would be no consent of the party who provided the information, because the information would then be introduced into evidence. If you call a witness, then I would say the Rule 70(B) limitations that is solely used for the purpose of generating new evidence, so apart from that information, does not apply anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To clarify, the issue is this: Any witness who is on our list who we intend to call and has given a statement to another entity, we have sought the permission of that provider to disclose those statements. That is a statement, for example, in other investigation. What we're looking at now is whether any material that we could view as Rule 68, in our view, and we are endeavouring to clarify that matter with providers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as I know, we have disclosed all prior statements of all witnesses on our list, as far as I can ascertain. So we've moved into a -- we've moved into a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're moving away from agreements with witnesses to testify, and we limit ourselves at this moment to the witness list. I mean, as soon as there is an agreement and there's a need to call a witness, we expect this - I'm sorry - we expect this witness to appear on the witness list as soon as possible. Is that -- I leave it to you, Mr. Re, and to you, Mr. Guy-Smith, to have a further conversation. We might need even a bit of a longer break. We'll hear from you and we'll then see whether the Chamber is in a position to decide on the motion; or whether we should rather wait. And if you would, at this moment, prefer to put the motion on hold, we'll hear from you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So we'll revisit the matter after the break. Then I move on to -- I think this completed item 3 on the agenda. Is there any other matter to be raised in relation to any motions? Mr. Emmerson? Mr. Guy-Smith? No, Mr. Harvey? Then we'll move on to item 4, which is mentioned, state of disclosure. Could I ask the parties, first of all, for an update. Mr. Re, could you update the Chamber with your views on the state of disclosure at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as I can ascertain, with Rule 66(A)(ii) [Realtime transcript read in error "68(A)(ii)"], there are two witnesses whose prior testimony is in the process of being disclosed. As far as I can ascertain, to the best of the searches which I have asked to be done, it appears that we have disclosed all prior statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to verify, did you say 66(A)(ii) or did you say 68? It's my recollection that you said 66, but I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the transcript it reads 68, so that should then be are corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are outstanding transcript in Albanian. There are 38 days of prior testimony of witnesses in Albanian which have to be cut onto tapes by the Registry and given back to us. Now, it's a matter for the Defence if they want the prior testimony on an Albanian tape or are content with the English transcripts which we've already disclosed to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter to update the Chamber upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With Rule 68, we have a system in place, we have searches; and as we find material, it's of course ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can approach this, if I may, with five bullet points. We've obviously reviewed all of the material that the Prosecution has served against its pre-trial brief. We believe that there are four or five -- four or possibly five statements which are referred to in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief which have not so far been disclosed to the Defence, and I will provide Mr. Re with a list of those witnesses during the course of the day. Secondly, Rule 65 ter exhibits. We have been working through the index provided by the Prosecution to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list to determine whether all of the material has been served on the disk provided by the Prosecution to accompany the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The documents that we have been able to copy and produce from the disk run, so far, to nine binders. Reviewing that against the exhibit list, there are just under 500 documents where the translations have not been provided, and there are a small number of documents where the originals and the translations have not been provided. Now, it is possible that some of those documents or translations may have been disclosed by the Prosecution in earlier batches of disclosure, although there is no obvious immediate means of cross-referencing the one to the other. It's obviously a relatively time-consuming exercise and it might be simpler, therefore, if the Prosecution were simply to supply to the Defence the remaining documents which are listed on its Rule 65 ter exhibit list that have not so far been served. Just to give Your Honours a flavor - and this is an issue I'm going to, if I may, come back to briefly under "Any Other Business" - we have already identified some important, or potentially important, and very lengthy exhibits, hundreds of pages, which have not been served and which relate to witnesses who are due to be called in the first week of the trial. I say they haven't been served. They had not been served until very late last night when, in response to chasing by the Defence, they are eventually disgorged. There's other material, we understand, on the way. But suffice to say, for present purposes, that the Rule 65 ter exhibits do not correspond with the list in full; and that it is clear that in some important respects and urgent ones, there are documents which have never been disclosed that are on the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, or translations that have never been disclosed. Thirdly, if I may, translations generally. There are a large number of potentially important contemporary documents for which translations do not exist. Examples include, and I've mentioned these before, all of the exhibits to the statements of General Bozidar Delic and General Dragan Zivanovic, the two JNA generals whose areas of operation intersected the region referred to in the indictment. Certainly, so far as General Delic is concerned, his witness statement as it stands does little more than to produce these exhibits, and without the exhibits his testimony is essentially incomprehensible. There are also a series of contemporary documents produced by Judge Radomir Gojkovic, the investigating judge tasked with the investigation of the late Radonjic Canal inquiry. Again, these documents remain untranslated. Now, we understand that the Prosecution has in its possession, and has had for some considerable time, unofficial translations of this material in English; and at the last 65 ter meeting on the 11th of January, the Prosecution agreed in terms to provide those unofficial translations to the Defence. They have not done so. Four, Rule 66(B). There are a number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just, for better understanding, under item 3, you said there were no translations of contemporary documents. Would that be -- would those be among the 500 not translated you mentioned under -- in relation to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The process of correlating the two is one which we will need to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- because it may be that some of the exhibits that are appended to the statements have not found their way into the Prosecution's exhibit list. But it's perfectly reasonable to assume that there will be a substantial element of cross-over between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. Please continue with number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 4, Rule 66(B) requests. There are a number of Rule 66(B) requests which have been outstanding for several months. Can I just give Your Honours one or two short examples. They are all recorded in correspondence between the parties. The Prosecution knows exactly which requests remain outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of other Rule 66(B) requests that remain outstanding --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Emmerson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and I'm very happy if it would assist Mr. Re to remind him of those passages, of those requests that remain outstanding, to provide him today or certainly tomorrow with an aide-memoire. But he's certainly aware from correspondence of the requests that have been made and that have not so far been met. The fifth and final point under this heading is that Mr. Re informed me yesterday that he is expecting a batch of material from Belgrade shortly. I have asked him to review this material urgently and to concentrate in particular on those witnesses who are due to give evidence in the first two weeks, because I think it may well be that in respect of at least one of those witnesses, the Prosecution has an outstanding request for the service of -- the provision of material from Belgrade. And we would obviously not wish to find ourselves in the position that that material was served either during or after the witness' testimony, or indeed immediately before. So those are the five bullet points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I fully concur in the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson. I have a bit of a concern. Over a year ago, in a 65 ter Conference, I indicated at that time that one of the most difficult and wearisome ways of trying a case is by being in a situation where there is late disclosure or ongoing disclosure as the case proceeds. It only -- I think it only causes more of a burden for the efficiency of a trial. At that time I suggested that there may come a time when Defence would ask for sanctions either by way of rulings of finding an adverse inference or the exclusion of evidence. I was scolded at the time and told that my concerns were somewhat premature. I find myself not yet in a position where I am asking for any sanctions, but I'm becoming increasingly more concerned about that. And I know the efforts that have been going on by Mr. Re, who has inherited this case from others, so I'm not laying the full responsibility at his feet. However, as we all understand, in a world where command responsibility is something that is well understood, it is now his army and he's responsible for it. My real concern comes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have to remind you of the case law before this Tribunal where a commander enters after the fact, that he's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not commenting on it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apart from Mr. Re not, for me, having the appearance of the commander. Let's keep it serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly don't intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood you well, that you have some compassion with someone who has to take over. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Part of my concern is this: With regard to the first two witnesses who are now contemplated, their statements were taken in 2002. That's five years ago or close to five, depending on what particular month. And there still is information with regard to their statements internally that has been in the possession of the Prosecution that we do not have. I was reviewing another witness, who we will see in the future. He is further down the line. He's presently identified as witness number 67. He's SST7/717. His statement was taken in 2004. There is an annex to his statement, and apparently he delivered a fair amount of information at that time to an investigator of the OTP. We don't have that information. I'm not at this point going to go through a laundry list of each and every witness in which I believe this problem exists; however, I think this is a problem that we may be visiting more often than any of us would like, and I don't know what the remedy is for. Some time ago in my previous tenure with the ADC, I had proposed a rule change involving the duty of the Prosecution to supply all this information months before a trial commences. I understand the difficulties that exist in the preparation of a trial for both sides; however, I am quite concerned that there are going to be substantial amounts of information given to us late in the day which will necessitate either a request for a break in the proceedings, some form of continuance, or, of necessity, longer examinations, because we will not have been in a position to integrate the information and focus on the information in a way that I know all of my colleagues would do. I don't have anything further to say at this time. I'm trying to set a marker here, and it's not a marker of criticism but more of concern, because I think it's going to dramatically affect the course and scope of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, your concern and your marker is on the record, and I do understand that you reserve your rights in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I share fully the concerns that have been raised by Mr. Guy-Smith and the specific bullet points that Mr. Emmerson has indicated to you. Oscar Wilde had famously said, "If I had longer, I would have been shorter." And the longer that we have to review these materials, the more concise, well-formulated and brief our questions will be. The delay in providing them places an enormous strain on all concerns and, indeed, on the Chamber's timetable. I don't think there's anything I can add; other than, if I do so, would put even further strain on the timetable. But it is something that has to be addressed as a matter of extreme urgency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Also for the new version of what I knew to be, "I did not find time to write you a shorter letter than this long one." Mr. Re, I'd like to give you an opportunity to respond after the break, because we'll need a break now; but before the break, I'd like to know -- Mr. Emmerson mentioned a batch of material from Belgrade, which I understand is newly to be disclosed. I may take it that you have not received that years and years ago but recently; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's more than newly to be disclosed; it's newly to be analysed. I am told that the material, the Serbian authorities we have requested -- sorry, we have requested material from the Serbian authorities, and it was arriving at the Belgrade office yesterday and was to be brought here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we are talking about a moment, it was received only a moment ago. Thank you. I'll give you an opportunity to respond to these concerns and these observations made by the Defence after the break. We'll adjourn until ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. If I might, before Mr. Re responds, I have been corrected by Mr. Willemsen with regard to one of the statements I made. I was looking at the wrong column with regard to SST7/17. I indicated there was information we did not have, and I misspoke myself. I should have said that there is information that we have not yet had translated. There are other individuals who could take that particular witness' place, but as I said before, I'm not going to go through a laundry list. So I wanted to correct the record in that regard so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. And it saves Mr. Re perhaps one or two lines in his response. Mr. Re, you have an opportunity to respond to various obligations and responses expressed in relation to disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution, of course, understands its obligations, and we understand and take very seriously the difficulties faced by the Defence in meeting the case. The system we have isn't a perfect system. We are endeavouring, and I'm endeavouring, to put in place better systems to enable us to identify all material that should be disclosed to the Defence and done so in a timely manner. Mr. Emmerson raised the matter of the translations and the in-house translations. A problem does exist within our internal system, and we are trying as hard as we can to identify all the internal translations; and if I had my way, I would have given them to the Defence on the same way. We haven't been able to do so. We are still trying to identify them and disclose them, and we are disclosing them as we identify them. I understand this isn't particularly acceptable, but I'm afraid that's all -- all we can do in the circumstances. In relation to the Delic matters, I am informed, and I am trying to put in place a system in which we can correctly identify all the material relating to General Delic. There are a number of documents referred to in his statement. A number of those have been translated in-house. We are still attempting to identify which ones they are and to get them to the Defence as soon as we possibly can. Now, it is, of course, in the interests of the efficient and smooth running of the trial, the Prosecution's interest, the Defence's interest, and the Trial Chamber's interest that we do so as soon as possible. Unfortunately, I cannot give a date for that. We have several people working on identifying this material and getting it into a -- and getting it to the Defence as soon as we can. In relation to the exhibit list and the number of translations, there are a number of duplicates on the exhibit list, the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. We are getting to a stage where we think we have identified almost all of the duplicates. We will have to file an updated list which, of course, with leave of the Tribunal -- Chamber, of course, and it will reflect translations which we have identified in-house and are no longer pending; it will identify duplicates and will identify those which we'll not rely upon because they are duplicates; and importantly, it will also identify a number of documents, many documents, which relate to the identification of, I think it was, 22 bodies in respect of whom we anticipate agreement with the Defence as to who the bodies -- whose bodies they were, and they will have to be -- and any documents relating to that will come off the list. So unfortunately, and I know it's -- all I can do is apologise for the lateness of this. We are, of course, looking at the first witnesses and whether any of those are affected by this. Mr. Emmerson correctly says that the documents coming from Serbia may impact upon one of the witnesses, and that would be on the list which I provided this morning, witness number 7 -- I'm sorry, witness number 8. It's the most likely witness in respect of whom Serbian documents may be applicable, but we won't know until we receive them and look at them, which we intend to do as soon as we get them, hopefully later today. Mr. Emmerson is providing us with a list of material which he -- which his team has identified as outstanding or there are translation issues. We will work on that as soon as we get it, and the Prosecution case managers will work with the Defence case managers to try and ameliorate the situation as best as we possibly can. In relation to K5 and K6, there is no impediment to providing the information to the Defence today - I've communicated that at least to Mr. Guy-Smith - and we'll get that to them today. Were there any other matters that Your Honours wished me to address?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that all Defence counsel will accept that material under the condition, as stipulated by Mr. Re, and if they feel there is any need to share the information outside the limited circle of the Defence teams, not including the accused, that they'll further address the matter. You well understand that the Chamber does understand that, I would say, usually counsel would receive such information in order to share it and discuss it with their clients, and that since there seems to be agreement on the conditions, that the Chamber is not bound in any way at a later stage to say, "Well, of course, for this and this reasons, you're entitled to share that with your --" We'll decide that on the merits of what you produce then, irrespective of the agreed limited disclosure, I must say, agreed among the parties. Of course, this -- the Chamber, of course, would not oppose any such disclosure at this moment. Whether that would be a kind of disclosure the Chamber would order if the Chamber would have been requested to make a ruling on it is a different matter. So if it ever comes to that, the Chamber will then hear whatever submission, irrespective of what the parties agreed upon at an earlier stage. Yes. If that's understood, then, of course, no ruling is needed at this moment. Just the parties proceed as they wish. And the mere fact that the Chamber has been informed about it is not in any way indicative of whether the Chamber considers this what a Chamber order could also contain. Then you said is there anything else. Well, Mr. Re, from what I -- of course I hear you speaking, I hear that we should improve the system; we are, of course, trying to do our utmost best. I didn't hear any expression of doubt, whether you did your utmost best. I think the issue might, sooner or later, be that when you say, "I am doing my best and the best can do no more," that the Defence would then say, "The best is not good enough." Of course, the Chamber might have more understanding for not having fully digested material received yesterday; whereas, the Chamber might have more difficulties in understanding that provisional translations, being made already quite some time ago, have not yet been identified as relevant to certain documents and therefore not being disclosed. I mean, that's -- but at this moment concerns have been expressed, and they are on the record. The Defence teams have reserved their rights and that's on the record as well, and, of course, the proof of the pudding is in the eating. We're all struggling with the huge amount of material in these kinds of cases, and I feel that there's mutual understanding for it. But as the French say, "To understand everything does not" -- I'll say it in French: "Tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner." "If you understand everything, then everything would be excused." That's, of course, not the case. That would not be the standard in this -- in these trials. Is there anything else specifically related to disclosure the parties would like to address at this moment? Because there have been some conversations during the break as well. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I think that leaves us with the remaining matter of UNMIK, and I think it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- fair to say that we need to have further discussions. I was going to actually try to use the new electronic system and publish a letter; but I think that if I read the letter, which is quite quick, it will explain to you a fair amount of the dilemma that we find ourselves in. This is a letter dated the 12th of February, and it is from UNMIK concerning disclosure requests that I had made. "Dear Mr. Guy-Smith, I refer to your three requests addressed to the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Joaquim Rucker, dated 5 and 6 February 2007, regarding the ICTY case against Ramush Haradinaj et al, in which you seek the disclosure of UNMIK CCIU police investigation files, as well as disclosure of protocols, guidelines, training, or other relevant manuals and instructions relevant to photo identification procedures used by UNMIK police investigators in their investigations related to the indictment against Ramush Haradinaj et al, to prepare the defence of your client, Mr. Idriz Balaj. "Consistent with the e-mail to you from Mr. George Huber dated 28 November 2006, in response to your request of 10 November 2006, for disclosure of materials provided by UNMIK to the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor (OTP), we do not make discovery to the Defence. The obligation to disclose evidence belongs exclusively to the ICTY Prosecutor. Accordingly, your request should be addressed to the OTP." This letter was in response to, obviously, a letter in which I'd asked for not only for general but specific information, which occurred after I had made a specific request to the OTP for disclosure of protocols, guidelines, training, or other relevant manuals and instructions relevant to photo identification procedures used by UNMIK police investigators, at a point in time when we were battling through the issue of photo identification and trying to get that particular part of the disclosure completed. I was told by the OTP and by Mr. Re quite kindly to refer my inquiries to UNMIK. UNMIK has told me to refer my inquiries to the Office of the Prosecutor. I've had a brief conversation with both Mr. Re and Mr. Dutertre during the break. I think that we may be able to cobble together some form of common approach to UNMIK. I'm not positive about that, but I think we probably will need a day or two, certainly over the weekend, and then we will probably report back to you on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, your suggestion is that the Chamber would not decide at this moment but give it another few days, to see whether a solution is found; if not, the Chamber will rule on the matter. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was one matter under 3(g), but I think that has been resolved as well. The disclosure to Defence counsel alone is not a need of a deadline anymore. Is that -- Mr. Re, may we understand that the agreement of disclosure, that is, K5 and K6, that that will take effect immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Today, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today, yes. So there's no need for a deadline there. We have completed agenda item 4, unless there is a need to further address disclosure issues. I do not see any request. Then, next item on the agenda, agreed facts. Is there any way to receive a joint report on agreed facts, either optimistic or pessimistic, but who can I give the floor? Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Your Honour may recall that we submitted a written report to the Trial Chamber on the 2nd of February, explaining what was then the state of progress on agreed facts proposals put forward by the Prosecution. In short, on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, we have responded in full to all of the agreed facts proposals which the Prosecution has so far put forward, and that leaves two matters outstanding. First, Your Honours are aware that the Defence served on Prosecution and, for information, on the Trial Chamber as well a set of proposed agreed facts addressing the military and political background to the case. That was served on the 15th of February. Those suggested agreed facts were drawn from statements and testimony of witnesses relied on by the Prosecution in this and other cases, and from the Prosecution's own statements about the military position in Kosovo in the Milosevic case and in the Milutinovic case. And they were, as Your Honours know, supported by a file of documents containing all the relevant citations and extracts to make the Prosecution's task of responding somewhat easier; and also in recognition of the fact that if agreement cannot be reached, the Defence may well, in due course, seek the admission of that material or, where appropriate, a ruling on adjudicated facts insofar as the material was drawn from adjudicated facts, particularly in the Limaj judgement. We are awaiting the Prosecution's response. The second issue relates to post mortem examinations. As we pointed out in the same report of the 5th of February, it has been agreed between the parties that the Prosecution would put forward to the Defence agreed facts proposals on the post mortem examinations conducted by international forensic pathologists following exhumations in 2002 and the successive years. In order for us to be able to respond to that material, obviously, we have to have the proposals, and as yet they have not been provided. The Prosecution has, as Your Honours know, provided expert witness statements and sought the response of the Defence and the response has been provided. But, in essence, the response is that the appropriate way of dealing with this is by way of agreed facts proposals for the reasons we have there set out, and there's been no indication from the Prosecution that they have altered their position that they will be producing agreed facts proposals. As I say, that was spelt out in our report of the 2nd of February and there's been no demure of that from the Prosecution. So those are the two outstanding matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, military matters and post mortem examinations. Any of the other Defence want to add anything? I see no response. Then, Mr. Re, no response yet on military matters and no proposals, as far as post mortem examinations are concerned. Would you please respond to what has been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. We have a proposal, a counter-proposal, ready to send to the Defence -- you can't hear me? Sorry. We have a proposal, a counter-proposal, ready to send to the Defence in relation to the agreed facts. I am confident we should be able to reach some form of agreement by tomorrow afternoon if we get it to them today. It will be in short form. The military one, my learned colleague, Mr. Emmerson, said the 15th of February. That doesn't quite accord with my recollection of when we received them. We can agree to a number of them. I'm sorry. I don't have the figure in front of me. It was there a moment ago and Mr. Di Fazio took the list with him when he took the court. I thought it was here. There are a percentage we can agree to. There are no agreement on those. We will be in a position to forward to the Defence a proposal tomorrow in relation to the military proposals which the Defence put forward. I would comment that some of them are things such as extracts from the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in the Milutinovic case or extracts of testimony by a witness, one witness or another, from other cases which have, of course, to be seen in context, in counter-distinction to the Prosecution's proposals which came from trial judgements or documents. So, in short, we'll have something back to the Defence by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the assistance of Judge Hoepfel, I am now "Access Denied for User Orie, A.," so I have some problems -- even in the favour of electronics, it does not always -- Yes. I think the wisest thing to do here is to wait for your proposal. There's nothing on our table yet to rule upon. At the same time, there's this song where you say three times, "Tomorrow, Tomorrow, Tomorrow." There's another song about "Yesterday." The Chamber prefers the second one. Yes, access is not any more denied. This completes 5, agreed facts, I would say. 6, the notification of a witness list, order of witnesses, proofing records, provision of witnesses -- witness statements to the Chamber. The Prosecution's witness list was filed as an annex to the Prosecution pre-trial brief on the 29th of January, and since then there have been changes to the list. I think we just received the most recent witness list. I think I saw it this morning, Mr. Re; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's basically the same as the one we e-mailed and sent to the Defence on the 7th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's two hours more than the previous one. It's basically the same but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. We've also -- we've e-mailed it now. It's in a spreadsheet. We've sorted it two ways. We've sorted it according to the order of testimony and the witness number. The one I handed round this morning is sorted according to -- only according to tentative order of testimony. I now have one which is sorted in order of witness number, the original number, that may assist, if I hand copies of those around to the Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do. With the assistance of the usher, I take it that you could distribute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. That's for the Chamber and that's for everyone else. There's one matter I would like to address in private session, if I could, at the appropriate point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it falls within the scope of the present item of the agenda, then we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Then let's see where we were on the agenda. Yes. We have now received the newest witness list. The Chamber, of course, on the basis of this new witness list, will have to decide what amount of hours will be granted to the Prosecution to present its case. We now have the relevant information on which we could make a ruling on that, and we might -- we might even do it today, but not -- of course, we first have to consider -- the changes are relatively small; therefore, our earlier deliberations will assist us in reaching final decisions. But nevertheless we'll take the next break to see if we can do that, yes or no. Then, next point is that the Trial Chamber has received the Prosecution's witness list for the first two weeks of trial, and we received that on the 25th of February by e-mail. Are there any changes in respect of this first two weeks' list?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The list which I handed out this morning reflects the current proposed order of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are two lists; one which says the "Tentative Order of Testimony," so there is one change from -- we notified that witness number 17, we were hoping to call number 1, if we could. So he is at number 17. That's the order of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's an international witness. You want to call him as a first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: These are the current plans, as good as we can get them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was at number 1, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The original list, we said subject to his government's approval. We've had to put him down the list by a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the list which is now sorted in the tentative order of testimony, that provides the information of the order of calling your witnesses. Any comments by any of the Defence teams? Yes. Is there any, now having discussed the order, is there anything else in relation to these first two weeks the parties of the Defence would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
