utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter or one cluster of matters which I was going to raise under "Any Other Business," but since Your Honour asked specifically in relation to the first witnesses, may I invite your attention to witnesses 1 and 2 on the Prosecution's tentative order of testimony. These witnesses -- and first is, as you see, a witness with protective measures currently in place. These witnesses are or were field workers for a non-governmental organisation based in Belgrade, operating in Kosovo. There are three points I need briefly to mention. First of all, the question of disclosure of material. I mentioned earlier that some six to 800 pages of material was disclosed for the first time very late last night. That relates to a lengthy report published by the organisation concerned of which hitherto only one page had been disclosed, and English translations of a number of notebooks compiled by the witness numbered 2 on the list. Those were all items that were on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. Now, without having seen the material, it's obviously very difficult for me to assess how much of it may, in fact, be relevant. When one looks at it, it may be very easy to hone in and identify a comparatively small number of pages that really need to be assimilated before cross-examination. So I make no submissions about the implications of that as at this present moment in time. But I'm sure Your Honour can see, given that we are three effective working days, including weekend working days, before the start of trial, that that is a matter I will need to review once we've had the opportunity to see what the material, in fact, represents. Secondly, in relation to both of those witnesses, it's right that I should put on -- put Your Honours on notice, so to speak, of the fact that there may well be issues concerning the admissibility of parts of the evidence of these two witnesses. If I can just, in a sentence or two, explain, because it has some procedural implications. Their statements contain a mixture of a limited amount of direct personal testimony of their own together with multiple hearsay, including summaries, sometimes sourced, sometimes not, of interviews with witnesses, some of whom are witnesses that the Prosecution is proposing to call in support of particular counts in the indictment viva voce. In some instances, they exhibit witness statements to their own statements, which are either taken by themselves, more often by field workers or by, indeed, the Serbian police, the MUP. Their own statements contain quite a considerable amount of unsourced hearsay and rumour, as well as a certain amount of opinion evidence. So they raise potentially complex questions of admissibility. I've discussed these issues with Mr. Re on a number of occasions, orally and in writing, and I have asked him now to identify precisely which parts of their evidence he intends to elicit. We are, I think, agreed that there is inadmissible and irrelevant material in their statements, but the Prosecution has not yet indicated which parts of their statements they do intend to rely on. And I raise this now because it may, first of all, be necessary to seek a ruling from the Trial Chamber on these witnesses, or parts of their testimony, before they are called; but I raise it also because as Your Honour, I think, will immediately see, the Defence are just not in a position at the moment to formulate or prepare their arguments on the admissibility of parts or all of the testimony the Prosecution proposes to adduce because the Prosecution has not given the Defence an indication of the testimony it does intend to adduce. That is something which needs to be rectified as a matter of urgency, because if opening speeches are to be made on Monday, it would be necessary to move into legal argument, if there is to be any, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I perhaps try to cut matters short. Mr. Re, I see that the witness list number 1 is scheduled for two hours; witness 2 is scheduled for two hours as well. If it is true that there are reports, only recently disclosed and relevant to the testimony of these witnesses, reports by the organisation they -- and if these reports are 800 pages, I take it that you do not imagine to go through all of these 800 pages with these witnesses in the two hours available for each of them. Is there any possibility for you to identify for the Defence those portions of the report you would specifically rely on as a factual basis for the examination of -- or at least relevant for facts you'd like to elicit from those --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Re replies. It may be that I didn't make my submissions quite as clearly as I should have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were two separate problems. One is the disclosure of material late last night. Like I say, I have no reason to believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just that it's logical to report --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That consists of the translations of four notebooks, which had previously been disclosed in Serbian, and the service of a 300-page report, which had previously been the subject only of the service of one page. Nobody at the moment knows how much, if any, of that material is relevant. Where the problem arises is in the witness statements themselves which, as I've indicated, contain this vast array of material of varying quality and reliability and which raise a number of potentially difficult issues of admissibility. And it's in respect of the witness statements that I have been asking the Prosecution to identify what it is they are proposing to adduce. Moreover, and I'll deal with this very briefly, I understand that Mr. Re had an interview or proofing session with the protected witness SST7/28 yesterday and plans another one over this weekend, and that Mr. Di Fazio has been dealing with proofing sessions with the second witness, Ms. Andjelkovic. We're obviously coming on to the disclosure of proofing notes as an issue on the agenda, but we would very much want to have the records of those sessions in sufficient time to be able to assimilate what it is exactly the Prosecution wants to elicit from these witnesses, in effect, paragraph by paragraph so we can formulate any objections that there may be. And of course there may not be in the end. At the moment we don't know what the Prosecution wants to elicit from these witnesses in sufficient detail to assess or analyse our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Both witnesses, in our submission, give accounts of what they observed and what they saw in Kosovo in 1998. These statements refer to matters outside the indictment period. Rest assured, of course the Prosecution is not going to elicit irrelevant evidence from these statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, just to keep matters short. I think Mr. Emmerson was not soliciting that you explain to the Chamber what you want to elicit from these witnesses but to the Defence. Of course, it's fine if you -- but what they are seeking is your assistance such that they know what to focus on in preparing for cross-examination. I think that's the issue, if I've understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is, a statement from the Prosecution of the evidence they intend to elicit in sufficient particularity to enable the Defence, A, to formulate objections to admissibility, because much of the material, on its face, is amenable to such objections and, B, of course, to prepare cross-examination. But at the moment -- and if Your Honours read the statements, you would see immediately that you have to pick through pages of material to find anything which, on its face, is admissible probative relevant first-hand testimony. The vast bulk of it is third-hand reports of what somebody else told somebody else when very often, in certain instances at least, the ultimate source of information isn't even identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "even," where he'd say this is not prohibited in this Tribunal, that here are strong reasons to argue this. This would be inadmissible --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not arguing for an absolute ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, of course, not. I couldn't give it at this moment; the Chamber could not give it at this moment. Mr. Re, well, of course, usually in order to know better what would be the focus of examination of a witness, of course, would be to look at the 65 ter summary because there you outline -- you do not perhaps necessarily repeat all of what is in the statement but what you want to elicit. Do I understand that the 65 ter summary does not give you sufficient guidance for --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is virtually of no use whatsoever for the purposes that I've outlined. The first 65 ter summary, that is of the second witness, contains material which simply refers, in very general terms but not in specific terms, to the categories involved, and the second one contains a much more detailed summary, obviously prepared by someone else, which includes all of the material Mr. Re referred to outside the indictment period. What I have done is I have written to Mr. Re and I have divided the witness statements collectively into seven different categories: Direct testimony, summaries of the statement of a witness who is to be called by the Prosecution, and so forth. And I have asked him to indicate which of those seven categories, in principle, he proposes to seek to elicit so that the legal position can be clarified; and then to identify which paragraphs of the statements he proposes to adduce. It's, I hope, a reasonable and, frankly, one without which we simply cannot formulate our position. I'm not asking for further time at the moment, but I am asking the Prosecution to state its position. It's chosen to call as its first two witnesses, witnesses whose statements raise extremely difficult questions of admissibility and reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, do you think that you could answer the request or reply to the request of Mr. Emmerson in such a way that he would be happy over the weekend, or at least on Monday, or do you think it's a matter which needs more attention at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer whether I can make Mr. Emmerson happy. We had this conversation yesterday over the phone. That's why when I started responding, Mr. Emmerson was rehearsing what he said yesterday and I was about to respond how I responded yesterday. I don't think we really need to trouble the Trial Chamber with inter partes conversations unless we get to the point where we can't resolve it. I have his letter. I am speaking to the witness. I spoke to her briefly yesterday, and I will be speaking to her on Sunday. The Defence is aware of that. When I have the results of that, I will produce it to him. We could not speak to her earlier for various logistical reasons for her and for us. Unfortunately, for the first week, that's just the way it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also understand from Mr. Emmerson that you had already some proofing sessions with at least one of these two witnesses. Is the results of those proofing sessions, are they already such that they could be made available, if at all, you want to make available to the Defence the reports of the proofing sessions. That's an outstanding matter. I remember there was some conversation about what the Defence, in the perfect world, not in the imperfect world, nevertheless, would like to have; that is, I remember 72 hours. I don't remember that it was ever a clear response of that from the Prosecution. But just now, the first proofing session, is that material available to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think proofing is a rather grand way of describing a telephone conversation I had for half an hour with the witness yesterday. I'm actually -- I'll actually be speaking to her in person in The Hague on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have started it. Her evidence, she will be referring to reports and her own observations. They're in her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I need to obtain from her, and started yesterday, was the source of her observations. She has told me that they are her own observations and those recorded in the reports. And it's general background information setting the pattern, setting the scene, for what happened in Kosovo. Yes, some of it is hearsay -- well, most of it is hearsay, but that's the nature of the introduction to these sorts of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the second one, witness number 2, Mr. Di Fazio is proofing her by videolink this afternoon, so I hope Mr. Di Fazio will be able to provide something to the Defence later today about what the second witness has said to them -- said to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do I understand, then, that later today we will receive a copy of the videolink of the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it has been recorded, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it raises -- there were two questions with regard to the issue of proofing which we seem to be fast approaching. One was when would we be receiving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the proofing and how it would be memorialised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first try to deal with the matter of the first two witnesses without, at this moment, entering into a kind of general debate on how we would have to deal with proofing sessions and when the results should be disclosed and how they should be recorded, et cetera, et cetera. The first question, quite simply, is: I do understand that until now the proofing session was limited to a telephone conversation of half an hour, and that further communication with this witness will take place this afternoon and Sunday. Are we -- is the Defence in a position to say, no, even if it was only half an hour, we have to be fully informed; or that you would say, well, this half an hour, let's wait and see what the more -- the larger proofing sessions or conversations will bring us; let us be informed about that and then let's see what needs we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I answer that question directly, I'm anxious, and I'm sure it's my fault, that we're aligning two different issues. One is the disclosure of records of proofing sessions, to which I'll return in a moment. The first is clarification of which aspects of the statements the Prosecution contends are admissible and should be admitted. Mr. Re says I communicated to him in writing yesterday. I'm sure he will agree that when we spoke on the 15th of February, as I indicated in my correspondence, I made a request for the clarification that I am now seeking. What I need in that respect is, as I have indicated, and it's quite separate from the proofing sessions. As regard the proofing sessions, Mr. Re has written to Mr. Guy-Smith to indicate that the Prosecution will, in general, seek to proof witnesses some considerable time before they are due to be called, and that records of those sessions will be disclosed as soon as they are available. That is the position of the Prosecution. So to that extent, that much at least is clear. As far as timing is concerned, it rather depends on what passed between Mr. Re and the witness during the half an hour that he spoke to her. If there was nothing more than general introductions and some parameters mapped out, then perhaps it wouldn't be of any value to the Defence to have it now. If, on the other hand, matters of substance were discussed, then perhaps the Defence ought to have it now. The real point is that as matters currently stand, Mr. Re will be proofing this witness on Sunday, presumably reducing that to writing, at best, on Sunday evening, serving it on Monday during the course of opening submissions, and calling the witness on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, against the background of admissibility issues that need to be raised and considered, it's an extremely short period of time, because it may well be the results of the proofing session will directly impact on whether the admissibility argument needs to be put forward and the form in which they take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I do understand Mr. Re to say, "We are inquiring into sources of knowledge," et cetera, et cetera, which suggests that at least it's not personal observation of events to take place. And you say, "Well, if we -- until now we have no knowledge, we have no information, about the sources; therefore, we cannot formulate any admissibility argument." At the same time, I also see that, whether we like it or not, that Mr. Re might not be in a position to come to you if he has not spoken to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just give Your Honour a practical example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One of these witnesses appends a collection of witness statements of other individuals to her witness statement, which includes statements made to the Serbian police, the MUP. One of those statements, certainly one of them, is a statement from a witness who is going to be called in these proceedings. Now, I understand from Mr. Re, because he has told me this in terms, that the Prosecution is not proposing to seek through these witnesses, so to speak, to introduce hearsay statements made by other witnesses that are appended to the witness statements of the two principal witnesses. So far, if I may say so, so good. But the actual content of the witness statements is itself a patchwork of summaries of either those statements or other statements not recorded or, in some instances, information provided through one step removed. Sometimes the source is recorded; sometimes it isn't. And with the greatest of respect, it does not take a proofing session for the Prosecution to apply some intellectual legal discipline to that statement and identify which parts of it, it says, can properly be adduced, paragraph by paragraph. And once that is done, the Defence can formulate its response. At the moment, I'm happy to do it on the basis that the Prosecution wants all these witness statements and their annexes adduced, but I know that isn't the position. And I don't want to waste the Trial Chamber's time or, indeed, the limited Defence preparation time in formulating arguments that, in due course, are going to prove to be unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you'd like to receive a copy saying this, this, this, this, that's what we'll focus on to start with; forget about the rest. That's one. And second is, if there's any hearsay without an identifiable source, that you'd like to receive information about the source as soon as it's available to Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, as I've indicated, we've divided the material in those statements into seven categories of principle, and I would like Mr. Re to indicate, as amongst those categories, which categories he contends ought properly to be admitted. I know that one of them he doesn't .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, I must repeat my words about making someone happy, but could you focus on the request made by Mr. Emmerson, focusing also on the identification of the parts you're already focusing on, and focusing on the additional information about the source of hearsay evidence? Could you -- do you think you could respond to that even without perhaps making Mr. Emmerson happy? I mean, do you say it's an useless exercise. Either choose them all, which doesn't help, or -- I mean, is this a failing communication or is it still worth the endeavour to see whether you could resolve this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a two-step process. Step one is what are we not relying upon. It's self-evident, I've told Mr. Emmerson. We're not relying upon anything which is outside the indictment period, any observations in the -- past September 1998. And the witness statements have got those, out. Witness statements appended, out. Step two is finding the source of all the information. I have started those inquiries. The witness has referred me to the reports. I'm trying to find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as you have solid information, you'll share that with Mr. Emmerson, in terms of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I'm doing. I am communicating with the witness. I have sent an e-mail to the witness asking to list some sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've told Mr. Emmerson that certain portions you will not rely on because they are outside the temporal scope of the -- which, of course, does not necessarily give an answer to what you focus on or what is still within the temporal scope of the indictment. Everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a witness who interviewed people in Kosovo as to what had happened to them or what they had seen and was there herself. And she has a colleague who gives similar evidence. It is the same as in any other case where human rights or -- sort of workers go into the field and make their observations through a mixture of interviews with refugees, people who live in villages, newspaper articles, and give their observations and their opinion as to the pattern. It's the usual, if I could put it in those terms, evidence of the widespread or systematic nature of an attack based upon their own personal observations and what they heard and saw. At the end of the day, it's a matter of weight for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you say it's rather broad. You also say, "I'll not rely on any information outside the temporal scope of the indictment." And did I also understand that you will not rely on any hearsay statements where the witnesses appear on the witness list to appear here, or is that untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In general, if a witness is on the list but has spoken to witness number 1, we will be submitting we would be permitted to lead evidence of the fact that they'd spoken, the general nature. What Mr. Emmerson was referring to, and what I told him we would not be reducing, is any contemporaneous statements witness number 1 took from witnesses on our witness lists. Those witnesses are here to give that evidence themselves, and it is of no value -- probative value to the Trial Chamber, unless it's a better record and it may assist -- the later witnesses' recollection. I don't propose to tender into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or undermine the later testimony of said witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's up to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just listening to that response, with the greatest of respect, illustrates the difficulties. On his feet, Mr. Re has just told Your Honours that he will not be seeking to introduce the written witness statement by X, who is going to be called to testify, but he does wish the witness to be able to give oral testimony of a summary of what the witness told her. So, in effect, he's adopting two contradictory positions in respect to the same piece of evidence, because the summary and the witness statement is drawn from the statement which is attached to the witness statement. And that is, if I may say so, a pristine illustration of the problems that we are facing in formulating a response to that. I don't want to be seen as though I am being nitpicking or being difficult. I am quite certain that were Your Honours to read these statements, you would immediately see the problem. It is not sufficient to simply say, "These are human rights workers and they are here to give general background." They are not tendered as expert witnesses giving evidence opinion; they are not apparently tendered to give hearsay statements, and yet in some effects they are. And cumulative effective statements, which may or may not be sourced, is then said to be the basis for an impressionistic opinion. Obviously, those are matters which can, some of them, properly go to weight at the end of the day. But the borderline of what goes to weight and what goes to proper admissibility is one which was explored, for example, by Judge Bonomy in the Milutinovic case in respect to material much better assembled and in a much disciplined and organisational fashion in a human rights report which was ultimately ruled inadmissible. In order to properly apply the Tribunal's jurisprudence, we have to know what the Prosecution wants to adduce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's of great use to continue this. The Chamber encourages the parties to meet on these matters, even if both parties are aware that they could not immediately resolve the matters, but to see whether a solution-oriented attitude could overcome the deadlock that seems not to be unrelated to a rather antagonistic approach at this time. I'm not blaming anyone for antagonistic approaches, but the Chamber would encourage you to see whether any progress could be made in this matter; and then, of course, we can't deal with the matter in any other way at this moment, not being fully performed. Then, of course, we'll see what happens and we'll see what rulings are required to be made next week. Yes. These are for the two witnesses. Now we have the other matter still remaining which is the memorandum of the 5th of February. Perhaps also we could not reach a final decision on whether proofing sessions should be -- well, there's, I take it, some agreement on disclosure of the results of proofing sessions, whether it be 72 hours or 48, or - what often happens in this Tribunal - 24 hours, we have from what I remember not a consolidated response to the suggestions made - at least, it has not been addressed to the Chamber - to the suggestions made to the Prosecution by the Defence. Wouldn't it be a wise first step to give a consolidated effort and say this is what you want, this is what we could consider what we could offer, and then we'll finally see where we end up. But such a consolidated response is not there yet, from what I understand. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not quite. The first week of -- the first week of witnesses has presented some logistical details -- difficulties. We are endeavouring at the moment, starting today, to proof witnesses in the week following and the week after. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- there's some difficulty with the first few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not blaming you, but we could accept this to be a pending matter for the next three or four months, and then of course we're already past the presentation of the Prosecution case so there's no need to resolve it anymore; or we could give it some priority to see what the position of the Prosecution is, the Defence has clarified its position in this respect, and see if we can create a kind of working system in which we don't have to argue the matter witness by witness but on a more general basis. Therefore, you're invited to provide a consolidated response to the proposals made in the 5th of February memo. I think it was that the Prosecution should provide the Trial Chamber the prior statements, who is to be called to testify viva voce, three clear working days before the witness is called. The Prosecution should provide to the Defence a record of any proofing sessions as early as possible, but at least five clear working days before the witness is expected to testify, and that is at least 48 hours before providing the statements of any such witness to the Trial Chamber. I mean, these are clear proposals. Whether you agree with them or not, let's see to what extent you could work out a solution; and if you don't find a solution, then of course the Chamber will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say this: If it assists, witness number 1, Sunday, proofing; witness number 2, today; witness number 3, Sunday; witness number 4, probably no proofing, trying to get travel documents. Of course she was only interviewed last month anyway. There won't be anything to add. Witness number 5, we're proofing him today by videolink; 6 and 7, don't know yet; 8, sometime next week. So we are in the process of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that's the timing, Mr. Re, but several issues have been raised; that is, when do we receive records of proofing sessions? Is the Prosecution in the position to give the statements to the Chamber, and at what moment? And should the Prosecution wait until it has given an opportunity to the Defence to comment on the proofing sessions and whether it's admissible or not, to send it to the Chamber? It's not just when will the witness be proofed, but it's also a matter of creating a system in which the parties know - and, of course, exceptions will always be there - but that we have at least a kind of schedule, a system, under which we operate. That's the issue. The proposals are there. Now the Defence is on notice of when the proofing of the first five or six witnesses will take place. But now it's elaborating a system in relation to the issues raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's an issue which, of course, would require an immediate, maybe, decision by the Trial Chamber and that is in relation to the furnishing of proofing notes. Now, clearly we give them to the Defence as soon as we -- as soon as we have them. The issue -- I mean, the Prosecution doesn't mind giving them to the Trial Chamber. The Defence may, of course, have their own opinion on whether we should provide them to the Trial Chamber. And that will start occurring today; that is, we will have proofing notes from today. So we are in the Trial Chamber's hands in relation to whether we provide them to you. We don't take -- we don't take a view. In relation to the statements, we don't take a view either on providing the statements. If the Trial Chamber wants the statements of the witnesses, we will, of course, provide them to you, according to whatever timetable you impose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just as an urgent solution, and irrespective of what we do later, we are now preparing for the next witness. If you receive proofing notes, let's say, by tomorrow, the first -- during the weekend, there ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would not be unhappy if it would receive whatever it said it would like to receive; that is, statements and proofing notes, to the extent that it comes to a kind of new statement - that's usually corrections to the original statements - by Monday, 12.00. This would give you an opportunity to at least have a couple of hours to say, "No, this should be barred from going to the Chamber because it is signed by the Queen of England rather than by the witness."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of principle, first of all, it seems to us that proofing notes are in the same category as witness statements; they are just, in effect, either a further statement either taken in full form or note form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how they are drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So as far as that slots into the template that we have suggested - and may I make it clear we never intended to suggest that that should be a template written in iron but a guideline - I mean, insofar as it would slot into the template, it would slot into the template at the time that the statements were generally provided to the Trial Chamber. Now, I appreciate that we're dealing with the truncated timetable perforce in the present circumstances, and one of the concerns the Defence has had, which Your Honour has rightly identified, is that what has happened over the last few days with very little service of material and then at late proofing material, it doesn't become ossified into a practice in the trial. As far as the first two witnesses are concerned, in one sense, I would -- those are examples of statements which I would, in general, be disposed to invite the Trial Chamber not to be looking at because of the vast amount of inadmissible and irrelevant material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, this Trial Chamber will have to decide admissibility; therefore, if you're thinking in terms of a jury system, it doesn't help. We have to look at it anyway, so that is not a reason to put --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was going to be my next sentence. In a sense, those are -- the points I've been making so far really will only become crystal clear, I think, to the Trial Chamber when they actually see the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In short, I'm happy with the proposal of 12 noon on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. And then you would emphasise that the Chamber might have to look at it primarily from a point of view of admissibility of that same material. Okay. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I clarify, is 12 noon the statements or the proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever you -- proofing notes, and there seems to be -- I don't know whether there's any disagreement. Proofing notes, taking the form of additions to the statements themselves. I mean, a proofing note could be, "We went through the whole of the statement of the witness and the witness said exactly the same as he said at that time." Then I would say the proofing note would be no changes whatsoever in the memory of the witness. It could also be that the witness says, "What I said was all lies because someone said I had to lie on this and this matters." Okay, then the proofing note will be rather short and then perhaps followed by some new information. It could also be that the witness says, "Everything's fine, but in that statement on that date, line 14, I mixed up Mr. A and Mr. B." Then, of course, it would take the form, more or less, of an additional statement which would be informative to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Proofing notes I understand, but the order for 12.00 Monday, does that also refer to the witnesses' statements as opposed to the proofing notes? When does the Trial Chamber want the statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the position of the Defence is that to provide these statements to the Chamber, and the admissibility of that, knowing that finally we'll see them anyhow, but whether or not they should be sent primarily for the purposes of argument on admissibility or just for our information to be prepared for the examination, that that may depend on what happens during the proofing sessions. That's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, as a general proposition. So far as these first two witnesses are concerned, the only reason I would suggest that we wait until Monday, 12 noon, for you to see the witness statements is because you have suggested that the parties should meet in an attempt to get some clarity about what exactly it is that the Prosecution seeks to elicit. Once that is done -- if, in fact, the statements that we have at the moment are largely redundant, and there are three or four or five or six paragraphs in them that the Prosecution really intends to adduce, then the matter can be dealt with in that way, perhaps with a fresh proofing note. But as a general proposition, I would have thought statements and proofing notes at the same time to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the size of the statements for the first two witnesses until now is approximately how many pages? I'm talking about statements, not about ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you include the annexes, which are the statements that they exhibit from other people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I suppose about -- a total of about 60 pages, is a guess. Maybe a bit more. A bit longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 187 -- 87 in total. That's for one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Monday, 12.00, for both statements and proofing notes is fine. Then, having dealt with this matter and expecting the Prosecution to respond in a more general way to the whole issue of when and what to produce, what to disclose at what moment, we have dealt with the matter for the first two witnesses. Then I would like to move on to the next item, and that is the approach to cross-examination. I think the Defence has suggested, I remember that, where the Chamber may have had 60 per cent in mind, 60 per cent of the time taken by examination-in-chief. But since this is a multiple-accused case, that for the Defence as a whole, they would prefer 80 to 100 per cent. The Chamber will follow that suggestion for the time being. Ninety is exactly in between 80 and 100, so that would be 90 per cent. The Chamber will be flexible in its approach on the condition that cross-examining counsel proceed in an efficient and helpful manner. Of course, how we will develop this standard very much depends on what we see and what we hear. At the same time, the Chamber would also like to thank you, Mr. Emmerson, as counsel for Mr. Haradinaj, for giving notice of witnesses for whom you expect to need a greater-than-average amount of time in cross-examination, as you gave to us on the 5th of February. That's highly appreciated. Any other matter in this respect, in cross-examination? Looking to you, Mr. Harvey, to you, Mr. Guy-Smith. That means that we have dealt with item 7 on the agenda. Item 8 is on the agenda since it has been requested by the Haradinaj Defence; that is, procedure for tendering exhibits. We had training again on e-court; I don't know whether you had that as well and whether that -- whether there are any remaining issues. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it may be that unless anybody has a particular issue to raise in that regard, that is not an issue that we need take time with at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber informs the parties that as far as technicalities are concerned, that we're struggling a bit with the status of documents once they have been presented to a witness, because we do understand that there are three, I would say, regular statuses; the one being marked for identification, that is, awaiting admission; the second is admitted and then it becomes an exhibit; and the third, tendered, not admitted. So that's also after the decision. Now, we do understand that there's a fourth category, that is, shown to a witness but without yet the express intent to tender that document as a -- to be admitted into evidence. The Chamber wonders whether that's not too complex for us and whether we should not, whenever a document is presented to a witness, that it gets the status of marked for identification. So unless there is a clear indication that counsel who is presenting that document to the witness has himself serious doubts as to whether or not he will tender that document into evidence -- it sometimes happens that there's one document floating around all the time, presented to every witness: "Do you recognise this document?" "No, I don't recognise that document" and then that's all. But, in principle, unless we have a clear indication of the opposite, the Chamber will assume that once a document is presented to a witness, that it's likely that it will be tendered into evidence. Another matter that we have considered is the matter of what to do with documents that are presented to witnesses, and if one of the parties claims that it should not be admitted into evidence, what the status of that document would be. There seems to be some concern, and the Chamber, in its training sessions, has also expressed concerns that it would still be on the record somewhere, where the Chamber itself decided that it would not look at it anymore because it is inadmissible evidence. The Chamber has understood that once we decide that a document, first marked for identification and then not admitted but for reasons the parties consider important for the Chamber not to look at it anymore ever in their lives, then you could withdraw the release of the document, which would result in a situation that it is on the record that a document which received a number, so an identifiable document, has been tendered, that admission was not granted, and that that's all on the record. The only thing we can't do anymore is to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Take it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can take it away. You can take it away by withdrawing the release, because a release of the document is a condition for handling it at all in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then finally, everything that would remain is what happened with that document, but we have no access to the document anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think providing the field which contained the document at the time it was marked for admission and given an exhibit number remains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That all remains. But if you want then to link to the document, you can't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can't do it. It's only if the field were removed that there would be a numbering crisis consequently with the exhibit numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the Chamber would like to convey to you, that we considered these matters. Is there anything else on the procedure of tendering exhibits? Not? Then we move on to item 9 of the agenda. We have understood that on Monday, the Prosecution will make an opening statement, and that the same is true for counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. We also understood, although we're not certain about the position of the Brahimaj Defence, that the other counsel will not make opening statements and that none of the accused will make a statement next Monday. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly, so far as I'm concerned, it is correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct. We will not be making an opening statement on whatever day it is after, and we reserve the right to make an opening statement at a later point in time if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the beginning of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I said, if it ever comes to that. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise for any confusion that may have resulted from an e-mail that I sent the other day to the Trial Chamber. It's merely that having spent last week together with my co-counsel. And may I pause and insert a parenthesis to introduce my co-counsel, Mr. Paul Troop, who was not able to be here earlier this morning but caught the first flight available. We welcome him to our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Close parenthesis. I would like to say that I would like an opportunity, as both Mr. Troop and I were in Kosovo last week, to have a final word with our client before closing the door. But I don't anticipate making an opening statement, and I will, of course, reserve my right to make a statement at the conclusion of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Under the rule, the statement, and disclosure of the Prosecution case, under rule -- I think the rule, as far as opening statements are concerned, that it leaves you the choice to make an opening statement at the beginning of the case or at the beginning of the presentation of the Defence case, which of course gives you an opportunity to file a 98 bis motion for an immediate acquittal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that would be in writing and would not be an oral statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I should have said at the opening of the Defence case and not at the closing of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you say that it is the same, the closure of the Prosecution case and the opening of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Should it be necessary, the opening of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. The Chamber in the present position expects the Prosecution to finish its presentation of its opening statement within two sessions. If we have three sessions in the morning, each of them a little bit less than one hour and a half, that stays within the time I think you claimed you need; and for Mr. Haradinaj's counsel, to finish your presentation in accordance with what you suggested, within one session, that would give you approximately one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At the moment the timing stands between one hour 15 and one hour 30, but I'm working to abbreviate it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so within one session; and then the Prosecution will be in a position to call its first witness on Tuesday, the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. That, of course, is subject to anything the Defence says about disclosure of information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- on Sunday, and we wouldn't object if the Defence were to say that we need an extra day or two to deal with it. We understand completely in those circumstances that these things might occur. You said a moment ago, Your Honour, two sessions. Is that -- the timing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's approximately three hours. On a day, we have from 9 to -- well, let's say, we have -- a morning session will take us from 9 to a quarter to 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take off two breaks, usually some 50 minutes, so a break on average to be 25 minutes. That's, therefore, a little bit over four hours. That makes three portions each, almost, one and a half hours. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I also just inform the Trial Chamber and the Defence that the Prosecutor herself, Madam Carla Del Ponte, wishes to commence the opening with a brief opening of maybe ten to 15 minutes, and then I will continue more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber leaves this to the parties who will act as counsel, and I think Madam Del Ponte is qualified to act as counsel on behalf of the Prosecution, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I may, because of what I understood Mr. Re to have said, if Madam Del Ponte is intending on making an opening statement and discussing, and appropriately, what an opening statement is confined to, that is fine. If she intends on doing something else, that raises an entirely different issue. This matter was actually, I believe, addressed in another proceeding at the Tribunal where the same attempt was made by the Prosecution's office, and specifically by Madam Del Ponte, and there was a concern voiced at that time that it was a political speech that was to be made as opposed to a statement with regard to the facts at hand. I raise this concern, only because I know that this is something which has happened before in the relatively recent past here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not have exactly in mind what you're alluding to, perhaps I not...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I'm informed about what seemed to have happened in the Popovic et al case, if that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this Chamber is aware that the Prosecutor in this Tribunal has several functions; of course, the primary function, to prosecute cases before this Tribunal. But it is understood that that needs context not focussing on what happens in the courtroom, and one could not deny that in context a political aspect will now and then element appear, if only because the Prosecutor is dealing with politicians now and then. I think it goes without saying, and I would not expect anything else, that Madam Del Ponte would clearly distinguish between what an opening statement means; that is, to give an overall impression to the Chamber and to the Defence of what the Prosecution intends to prove, the means by which it will prove it, perhaps to deal with legal issues, et cetera, and not to be a statement primarily of a political nature, mainly addressing the outside world, and if it would lose its character of being of assistance to the Chamber. On the other hand, Mr. Guy-Smith, we are old enough to know that these kinds of cases involving accused, sometimes with a political background as well, these kinds of cases in which we find often a mixture of individual behaviour but sometimes linked to political aspirations - I'm not saying in this case - but to draw the line between pointing at and addressing political elements involved in the case and political statements is not always that easy to draw exactly where that line is. But, of course, this Chamber could not expect anything else from the Prosecutor before this Tribunal to wisely find that line for herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate your remarks, Your Honour, and I think my suggestion may be a bit bolder than the Chamber is inclined to follow because of what I would take from your remarks to be, if nothing else, a gentle admonition to Madam Del Ponte of how to comport herself with regard to any opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't even call it an admonition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am sorry, a gentle statement, then. I think you have pointed out that well she does have a format side of the courtroom if she does choose to make any form of political statement. This is, as we are all quite aware, not a political trial but a criminal one. I was going to suggest that perhaps in the event she does choose to make an opening statement, or the first part of an only statement, that she present such remarks to the Chamber so that you can make a prior determination of whether or not it does, in fact, comport with the principles that you've articulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I raise this for a very specific reason, Your Honour. I can count on one hand the number of times that I have ever stood up and objected to an opening statement being made by an opponent. I find it something that is not particularly beneficial, nor is it something that I particularly care to do, and I don't want to be in a position where I'm doing that here because of the concerns I have and the rights that have to be protected. So I'm trying to fashion not only a remedy, if this is going to be the procedure, where two people from the Prosecutor's Office are going to make a statement, but also because of the concerns that I have. And I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. Since it is an issue that has been raised now two minutes ago, I suggest that, first of all, you speak with Mr. Re to see whether your concern is justified in any way. We'll adjourn at this moment. Mr. Re, you'll have an opportunity to respond to that after the break, and I do not expect anything else to be discussed after the break then; perhaps this issue but very briefly. Second, the Chamber might come with a decision on the time granted to the Prosecution to present its case. Therefore, we'll stand adjourned -- Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit concerned about interpreters and technicians, so therefore if it is a matter that could be left until after the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, if Your Honour is happy, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd suggest that we take a break for 25 minutes, that we resume at 1.25, and it should be clear to everyone that we have then only a limited time left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two matters remaining on our agenda, the second one being a decision by the Trial Chamber on the time to be granted to the Prosecution to present its case; and the first one, whether there are any additional observations to be made in relation to Madam Del Ponte participating in the opening statement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, Madam Del Ponte, wishes to open the case, to initiate the opening, to underscore the importance she personally places on these proceedings and the fact that they have got so far. The Prosecutor is, of course, fully aware of the line between political and legal statements. The Prosecutor is entitled to make a statement before the Chamber. There is no provision in the rules permitting or allowing Defence counsel to vet the opening statement after submitting it to them for approval of either party, Prosecution or Defence. The Prosecutor certainly doesn't propose to submit to Mr. Guy-Smith or anyone else her opening statement for approval or vetting in advance. And a suggestion that she would come in here and make a political statement as opposed to a legal statement addressed to the case itself is, or could be construed as, an attack upon her integrity as a prosecutor, and she fully refutes any such suggestion. Rest assured, the Prosecutor intends to address the Trial Chamber on matters relating to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to respond to that, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I don't need to respond to that, but under the general rubric of this item, we had previously indicated that though we were making an opening statement, it wasn't anticipated that Mr. Haradinaj would be making an opening statement under Rule 84 bis. He has now wishes to reconsider his position in light of the Prosecutor's decision to open the case light; and if he does make a statement, it will be a short one, a very short one, not one which will, in any way, affect the overall time frame that I have already outlined to the Trial Chamber. Insofar as he would wish to make a statement, it will be a statement that will be within the time frame that I have indicated. Secondly, he would request, and I would request on his behalf, that Ms. Del Ponte, if she was to take part in the opening proceedings, be present to hear his statement, and not to depart the proceedings after she has made her own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think the remarks made by Mr. Re point out the precise problem. "Whatever importance she personally places on these proceedings and the fact that they have gotten so far" is something she can do outside of the courtroom, not inside of the courtroom. I certainly wasn't suggesting that I vet her statement, if she wishes to give it to me. I'm more than happy to look at it in whatever language she submits it in. I was suggesting rather that the Chamber make that determination. Finally, with regard to her integrity, I make no comment whatsoever. I certainly wasn't intending, by these remarks, to make any comments about her integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the change of mind of Mr. Haradinaj is, to system extent, surprising because it suggests, more or less, that an opening statement would be any different if -- depending on whether Mr. Re addresses this Chamber or whether Madam Del Ponte addresses this Chamber. And I think that I'd been clear before the break that if Madam Del Ponte chooses to represent the Prosecution during the opening statement, showing a particular interest in this case by her mere presence, how that could trigger, apart from the presence of Mr. Haradinaj - well, he's present anyhow - but finally, Mr. Haradinaj is entitled to make such a statement, at least we can allow it. I am not deciding at this moment whether this late change of mind, and the reason given for it, would make the decide to allow such a situation. I have to look at the rules Chamber to look at the rules very precisely also. It should be under the -- let me just have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it's page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "If he or she so wishes, and the Trial Chamber so decides," so such a decision is not there at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Further, I may draw your attention to the fact that such a statement is under the control of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, just as some concern was expressed by Mr. Guy-Smith that I could not exclude for full 100 per cent that concerns about the content of a statement, I would say more or less, in response to Madam Del Ponte's participation in an opening statement, might not come up for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we'll consider the matter and let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one matter. It's not that -- entirely right to say that there was -- that this is a situation in which there was a firmly settled position communicated to the Trial Chamber. The matter has been under review all work. A provisional decision had been taken, and among the factors that have unquestionably borne on Mr. Haradinaj's decision-making is this latest development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that, and the Prosecutorial situation is quite clear. There's no decision yet. And we'll consider the matter. Of course, it may be clear, also from my previous observations, that although the Chamber is aware that, unlike in common theft cases in Winbourne, that these cases here cannot be denied to have, not in its adjudication but its context, sometimes some political elements. The functioning of this Tribunal is discussed often by politicians. Politicians are sometimes addressed by those representing organs of this Tribunal. Also, from what I learned from the media is that politicians draw consequences of what happens in and outside this Tribunal but related to this Tribunal. This Chamber wants to focus on adjudication of charges brought against individuals. That's what our focus is on, not on political precursors, not on political effects, not on political discussions. Mr. Emmerson, I'm certain that to the extent at that Mr. Haradinaj, whom I understand has a political career to the extent that he doesn't understand that yet, that you certainly could assist him in understanding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think he does understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the second issue, and let me just see -- this Chamber does not feel that it is in a position to -- not only not to instruct, well, even not to guide the Prosecutor of this Tribunal how to spend her time. If she considers it of importance to participate in the opening statement delivered by the Prosecution and then decides that she has other things to do and therefore either follow from a distance what happens in these proceedings or do other things being reported about at a later stage, that Madam Del Ponte is entirely free to do so. And I don't know to whom the request was addressed that she'd stay and hear Mr. Haradinaj's submissions. If it was addressed to the Chamber, the answer would have been -- if it's directly addressed to her, then Mr. Re will consider whether or not to convey this to Madam Del Ponte or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I was certainly not asking to invoke the Tribunal's jurisdiction to issue an order of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But it is a request that would be addressed to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are on the same line as far as the legal aspects are concerned. Those are the only ones that do concern the Chamber. That's as far as the opening statement is concerned. Mr. Re, for your information, you have certainly observed my total ignorance on what happened in the Popovic case. I know now what happened on the 14th of July, 2006. I'll read what happened there because it seems to have raised some concerns with Mr. Guy-Smith, so I think this it's wise to better understand what caused his concerns. Then I'm not raised in the system applied here, I'm not raised in a system where the opening statement are the start of a case. Therefore, over this weekend, I'll better inform myself. Although I have a general knowledge of what an opening statement is for in the tradition where it's usually applied, I'll further orient myself on what is an opening statement. Madam Del Ponte is working already for such a long time here that even if she might be in a similar situation as I am, that is, not be familiar with opening statements in her own system -- unfortunately, in Switzerland, every canton has its own system of criminal procedures. I would have no idea whether she was familiar with it already from her past. But I have no doubt that she still -- or irrespective of whether she had already an appropriate -- not an appropriate, had already a thorough knowledge of what an opening statement is for, that she certainly would have acquired that during the many, many years that she has already worked in this Tribunal. So I'll try to catch up with her so that we're here in a common understanding of what an opening statement is for. Then, the second issue, time for the presentation of the Prosecution case. On the basis of the information you have provided until now, the Chamber grants the Prosecution 175 hours examination-in-chief to present its case. This is not to encourage the use of 175 hours if less would do, and this is not a decision for eternity. As I said before today, the Chamber will take a flexible approach and will also look at how the time is used and reserve all rights to adapt the number of hours granted if good cause exists to do so. Is there any other matter to be raised at this moment? I don't see any applications. Then I'd like to thank the parties for their cooperative attitude and their efficient way of assisting the Chamber in performing its duties. We'll adjourn until -- it's good that I am stopped for a -- because there are matters that will take not more than one minute. First of all, the parties are informed that the Chamber envisages at this moment not to sit on the 29th and the 30th of March. It's not definitive, but that's what we envisage will happen. It will not sit - but also there changes are possible - from the 10th to the 13th of April; from the 1st to the 4th of May; May 25th; the 8th of June; the 23rd to the 27th of July. And it may not be a secret to you that the 6th and the 9th and the 30th of April are UN holidays; therefore, not sitting. The same is true for the 28th of May. Finally, the parties are informed that for reasons of economy, that the Prosecution witnesses will be referred to by the final number in their pseudonyms. For example, Witness SST7/65 will be referred to simply as Witness 65, unless there's any reason to give further details. Since there are no matters -- no other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until Monday, the 4th of March, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
